The material investigated was a new high gamma-prime content polycrystalline nickel-based alloy, referred to as Alloy 11.
The as-forged microstructure of Alloy 11 exhibited a trimodal distribution of gamma-prime precipitates: primary (mean size 430 nm), secondary (mean size 76 nm), and tertiary (mean size 25 nm).
In-situ heating of the thin TEM lamella samples was performed in a STEM from room temperature up to 1150°C, with EELS analysis conducted at each temperature step.
The dissolution of the tertiary gamma-prime precipitates was observed to initiate at lower temperatures than the secondary gamma-prime precipitates.

The authors used the Gibbs-Thomson relation and the reversed-growth approximation to explain the faster dissolution of the smaller tertiary gamma-prime precipitates compared to the larger secondary gamma-prime precipitates.

The EELS data analysis employed a model-based quantification approach to improve accuracy, incorporating plural scattering effects while excluding the analysis of electron loss near-edge fine-structure (ELNES) features.
The in-situ STEM-EELS approach provided high-resolution local information on the compositional evolution of the different gamma-prime precipitate populations during heating.
The findings have important implications for optimizing heat treatment schedules to maintain the desired microstructure and properties of nickel-based superalloys.
The authors noted that the small interaction volume and reduced diffusion paths in the thin TEM samples may have led to accelerated diffusional phenomena compared to the bulk material.
The observations of the different dissolution behavior of secondary and primary gamma-prime precipitates were consistent with previous studies using techniques like differential thermal analysis.
The material analyzed was obtained from a pancake forging of Alloy 11, produced by isothermally forging a powder isostatic pressed cylindrical compact.
The thin TEM lamella samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) system with an optimized thinning technique to minimize FIB-induced damage.
The in-situ heating experiments were performed using a DENSsolutions heating chip mounted on a 45° pre-tilted support, with temperature accuracy better than 5%.
The STEM-EELS analysis was carried out using a probe-corrected JEOL ARM200CF microscope operated at 200 kV, with a Gatan Quantum Dual EELS spectrometer.
The EELS data analysis and quantification were performed using the Gatan Microscopy Suite (GMS) software, with model-based quantification to improve accuracy.
